name: BaByliss trimmers/stylers
summary: A French-origin, Conair-owned brand of clippers, trimmers and hot tools; grooming gear with no appearance-outcome studies.
lead: BaByliss is a French personal care brand, now owned by the American group Conair, that sells hair dryers, curling irons, straighteners and, under its professional and men's lines, hair clippers and beard trimmers . Within grooming discussions, its trimmers and stylers are one of several professional-style tool brands.

name: Remington IPL home device
summary: Remington's home IPL flasher: reduces hair over repeated sessions on light-to-medium skin, no device-specific trials.
lead: Remington sells home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal devices under its iLight line. IPL uses broad-spectrum light absorbed by melanin in the hair to heat and damage the follicle, and repeated sessions are needed because only follicles in the growth phase respond.

name: Veet depilatory cream
summary: Chemical hair-dissolving cream from Reckitt: fast, painless-at-the-surface hair removal that regrows in days.
lead: Veet is a brand of chemical depilatory products, mainly creams, lotions and gels, that remove body hair by dissolving the keratin of the hair shaft so it can be wiped off at the skin surface. It is owned by Reckitt Benckiser and traces its origin to a Canadian product sold under the name Neet from 1919.

name: Nair depilatory
summary: Classic drugstore depilatory cream: dissolves hair at the surface, regrows in days, irritation is the main caveat.
lead: Nair is an American brand of chemical depilatory products, including creams, lotions and sprays, that remove hair by breaking down keratin so it can be wiped from the skin. According to Wikipedia, the original lotion launched in 1940 and the brand is now owned by Church & Dwight, which bought it from Carter-Wallace in 2001.

name: Manscaped trimmers
summary: Heavily marketed men's body-grooming trimmer brand; criticised for premium pricing.
lead: Manscaped is a San Diego direct-to-consumer brand of men's grooming tools, founded in 2016 by Paul Tran and Steve King, best known for the Lawn Mower electric trimmer for body and pubic hair.

name: Electric tweezers
summary: Battery-powered pluckers, some sold with a claim of damaging the root; no human studies found.
lead: Electric tweezers is a name used for two different things: powered tweezers (a motor-driven gripping tool, covered by patents such as a 2006 filing for a motorised tweezer) and, in hair removal, tweezers that pass an electrical signal through the tip to damage the hair root so it does not regrow. Wikipedia describes the latter as an intended method of depilation.

name: Braun Silk-expert IPL
summary: Braun's home IPL with a skin-tone sensor: sensor-limited safety, no device-specific trials found.
lead: Braun Silk-expert is Braun's home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal line, with versions described as having a skin-tone sensor. Braun is a Procter & Gamble subsidiary, and Wikipedia lists IPL appliances and epilators among its beauty-care products.

name: Philips Lumea
summary: Philips home IPL hair-removal device; the category has some trial support for hair reduction, but evidence specific to this model is thin.
lead: The Philips Lumea is a handheld consumer device for hair removal at home using intense pulsed light (IPL). It is one of several home IPL products sold as an alternative to treatment in a clinic.

name: Tria Beauty hair removal laser
summary: An at-home diode laser for hair reduction, one of two over-the-counter diode devices the FDA had cleared as of 2025.
lead: The Tria is a hair-removal diode laser sold for home use. Wikipedia states that, as of 2025, the US FDA had cleared two diode devices for over-the-counter sale, the Epilaser and the TRIA.

name: Silk'n Infinity / Flash&Go
summary: Silk'n home light-based hair-removal devices; an early small study of the brand's home pulsed light device reported hair reduction.
lead: Silk'n is a brand of home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go models. An early device from the brand, made by HomeSkinovations of Israel, was described in a 2009 study as a small, light-weight, low-energy, low-cost IPL system for home use.

name: Magic Shave
summary: A chemical depilatory powder that dissolves hair at the skin surface; medical literature records eye injuries and a barium sulfide poisoning case.
lead: Magic Shave is a brand of chemical depilatory powder. Wikipedia lists it, alongside Nair and Veet, among depilatory products sold as gels, creams, lotions, aerosols, roll-ons and powders.

name: Laser hair-growth helmet/cap
summary: Wearable low-level laser caps and helmets marketed for androgenetic alopecia; reviews report mixed-to-tentative benefit and call for larger trials.
lead: Laser hair-growth helmets and caps are wearable devices that apply low-level laser therapy (LLLT, also called photobiomodulation) to the scalp with the aim of treating androgenetic alopecia. Wikipedia lists hats, combs and helmets among home-use LLLT options.
claims: A laser helmet has a stronger regrowth effect than other treatments

name: Hair fibres (Toppik)
summary: Keratin-style cosmetic fibres that cling to existing hair to disguise thinning; a cover-up rather than a treatment, with a rare eye-injury case report.
lead: Hair fibres, sold under brands such as Toppik, are cosmetic products made of fine fibres that adhere to the hair shaft by electrostatic attraction to disguise hair loss in men and women.

name: Anthralin (dithranol)
summary: A skin-irritant ointment from psoriasis care that is sometimes discussed for patchy alopecia areata; evidence for hair regrowth is tentative.
lead: Anthralin, also called dithranol, is a synthetic topical compound from the hydroxyanthrone and anthracene family, supplied as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%. Its main established medical use is plaque psoriasis . In hair-related contexts it is discussed as a topical irritant treatment for alopecia areata, an autoimmune patchy hair-loss condition.

name: Coppertone sunscreen
summary: Classic U.S. sunscreen and suntan-lotion brand famous for its pigtailed-girl ad; brand-specific clinical evidence is essentially absent.
lead: Coppertone is a U.S. sun care brand. According to Wikipedia, it traces to a suntan lotion developed by pharmacist Benjamin Green in 1944, and it is described as the leading U.S. sun care brand . Its early marketing centred on tanning (slogan 'Tan, don't burn') rather than sunscreen as such .

name: Piz Buin
summary: Alpine-named European sun care brand dating to a 1946 glacier cream; only old mouse studies exist.
lead: Piz Buin is a European sun care brand. According to Wikipedia, Austrian chemist Franz Greiter introduced a product called Gletscher Crème in 1946 that became the basis for Piz Buin, named after the mountain where Greiter reportedly got sunburned .

name: Bain de Soleil
summary: Discontinued 1925-born French-American tanning gel brand known for low SPF and nostalgia; no clinical evidence behind it.
lead: Bain de Soleil ('sun bath' in French) was a tanning and sun care brand best known for an orange gel and low-SPF products. Wikipedia dates its origin to 1925, when Paris hairdresser Monsieur Antoine developed an orange gel tanning formula; Lanvin later introduced it in the U.S. . Bayer discontinued the brand in December 2019 .

name: Boots Soltan / star rating
summary: UK/Ireland star label showing a sunscreen's UVA-to-UVB protection ratio, from Boots.
lead: The Boots star rating is a UK and Ireland labelling system for the UVA protection of sunscreens, expressed relative to UVB protection. Wikipedia describes it as a proprietary in vitro method in which five stars is the highest UVA ratio and one star the lowest . Soltan is a sunscreen range from Boots; the sources reviewed do not describe it.

name: Tinosorb S (bemotrizinol)
summary: A photostable broad-spectrum UV filter common in EU and Asian sunscreens, with US availability still pending in the sources reviewed.
lead: Bemotrizinol, sold by BASF as Tinosorb S and known by the INCI name bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine, is an oil-soluble organic ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens and daily skincare. It absorbs across the UVB and UVA ranges, with absorption peaks reported near 310 nm and 340-345 nm.

name: Tinosorb M (bisoctrizole)
summary: A hybrid organic/particulate UV filter in European and Asian sunscreens; reported contact allergies have been traced to a surfactant in its dispersion.
lead: Bisoctrizole, marketed by BASF as Tinosorb M (INCI name methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol), is an ultraviolet filter described as a hybrid: it is a benzotriazole organic molecule supplied as microfine particles in water-based dispersions, so it is said to act both by absorbing and by scattering UV light. It is used in sunscreens for broad UVA and UVB coverage.

name: Uvinul A Plus
summary: A photostable organic UVA filter used in EU sunscreens, with little published beyond chemistry and metabolism.
lead: Uvinul A Plus is BASF's trade name for diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB, also sold as Parsol DHHB), an organic UVA-absorbing sunscreen filter. It is described as photostable and is used in sunscreens and other cosmetics in the European Union at up to 10 percent.

name: Uvinul T 150 (ethylhexyl triazone)
summary: A UVB sunscreen filter used to boost SPF in EU products, with little published beyond formulation and environmental studies.
lead: Ethylhexyl triazone, marketed by BASF as Uvinul T 150, is an oil-soluble organic UVB filter used in sunscreens, typically to raise SPF. A Grokipedia summary reports an absorption peak near 314 nm, a permitted EU level of up to 5 percent, and no approval as a US sunscreen active.

name: Mexoryl SX (ecamsule)
summary: L'Oreal's long-studied UVA filter, with human photoprotection and absorption data.
lead: Ecamsule, known commercially as Mexoryl SX (INCI name terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid), is a water-soluble UVA filter developed by L'Oreal. Grokipedia states it absorbs with a peak near 345 nm and was developed and patented in 1982.

name: Mexoryl XL (drometrizole trisiloxane)
summary: L'Oreal's broad UVA/UVB filter, usually paired with Mexoryl SX; sold outside the US with little standalone research.
lead: Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold by L'Oreal as Mexoryl XL, is a lipophilic benzotriazole-derived UV filter that absorbs in both UVB and UVA, with peaks reported at 303 nm and 344 nm. It is often combined with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX).

name: Iscotrizinol (Uvasorb HEB)
summary: A very photostable triazine UVB filter common in East Asian sunscreens, with little human clinical research under its own name.
lead: Iscotrizinol, listed in ingredient labels as diethylhexyl butamido triazone and sold under the trade name Uvasorb HEB, is an organic (chemical) ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens. It belongs to the triazine family, absorbs mainly UVB and some short-wave UVA light, and has its peak absorption near 310 nm.

name: Parsol 1789 (avobenzone)
summary: The standard UVA filter in most chemical sunscreens, effective but needing stabilizers because it degrades in sunlight.
lead: Avobenzone, sold under trade names including Parsol 1789, Eusolex 9020 and Escalol 517, is an oil-soluble organic filter used in sunscreens to absorb ultraviolet A (UVA) light, with peak absorption near 357 to 360 nm. It is a dibenzoylmethane derivative with the formula C20H22O3.

name: Octocrylene
summary: A photostable UVB filter used mainly to keep avobenzone from breaking down, with open questions over absorption, benzophenone formation and reef effects.
lead: Octocrylene is an organic ultraviolet filter and photostabilizer used in sunscreens and other cosmetics. It is an ester (C24H27NO2) that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light, and it is commonly added to stabilize avobenzone.

name: Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen
summary: A photostable broad-spectrum mineral sunscreen filter, FDA-GRASE, whose main trade-off is white cast and nanoparticle debate.
lead: Zinc oxide mineral sunscreen uses zinc oxide, an inorganic (mineral) compound, as its active ultraviolet filter. Zinc oxide protects against both UVA and UVB light and, with titanium dioxide, is one of the two mineral filters used in sunscreens.

name: Titanium dioxide sunscreen
summary: A mineral UV filter, FDA-GRASE, strong on UVB and partly UVA, usually paired with zinc oxide.
lead: Titanium dioxide sunscreen uses titanium dioxide (TiO2), an inorganic mineral, as an ultraviolet filter. With zinc oxide it is one of the two mineral filters in sunscreens, and the two were the only filters the US FDA classed as generally recognized as safe and effective as of 2021.

name: Oxybenzone-free sunscreen
summary: A label category for sunscreens without benzophenone-3, driven by allergy, hormone and reef concerns that are debated.
lead: Oxybenzone-free sunscreen refers to sunscreens formulated without oxybenzone (benzophenone-3, BP-3), an organic UV filter that has been the subject of safety and environmental debate. The term is a marketing and consumer category rather than a single ingredient.
